long.q: Name the type of reaction: (a) 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂ (heated with MnO₂); (b) NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O; (c) 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.

long.q: Distinguish between temporary and permanent hardness of water and state, with an equation, how each is removed.

long.q: Give reasons: (a) fish cannot live in water that has been boiled and cooled; (b) hard water wastes soap; (c) white anhydrous copper sulphate turns blue when water is added.
scheme: B1: boiling drives out the dissolved oxygen that fish need to breathe

B1: it combines with water to form hydrated copper sulphate, CuSO₄·5H₂O, which is blue

long.q: Calculate the percentage of water of crystallisation in washing soda, Na₂CO₃·10H₂O. (Na = 23, C = 12, O = 16, H = 1)
scheme: C1: 10H₂O = 180, so molecular mass = 286
M1: percentage of water = (180 ÷ 286) × 100

long.q: State two postulates of Bohr's model of the atom.
scheme: B1: electrons revolve round the nucleus in fixed circular orbits (shells or energy levels) without losing energy
B1: an electron absorbs or gives out energy only when it jumps from one orbit to another

long.q: Chlorine contains 75 % of the isotope ³⁵Cl and 25 % of ³⁷Cl. Calculate the average atomic mass of chlorine.
scheme: M1: average atomic mass = (35 × 75 + 37 × 25) ÷ 100

long.q: Describe in words the formation of magnesium chloride from magnesium (atomic number 12) and chlorine (atomic number 17).
scheme: B1: magnesium (2, 8, 2) loses its two valence electrons to form Mg²⁺ (2, 8)
B1: each of two chlorine atoms (2, 8, 7) gains one electron to form Cl⁻ (2, 8, 8)
B1: both ions now have the stable octet of a noble gas (neon and argon)
B1: the oppositely charged ions are held together by strong electrostatic attraction, forming the electrovalent compound MgCl₂

long.q: Describe in words how covalent bonds are formed in a water molecule.
scheme: B1: oxygen (2, 6) needs two more electrons, and each hydrogen atom has one electron
B1: the oxygen atom shares one pair of electrons with each of the two hydrogen atoms
B1: this gives two single covalent bonds; oxygen completes its octet with two lone pairs left, and each hydrogen gets a duplet

long.q: State four differences in the properties of electrovalent and covalent compounds.
scheme: B1: electrovalent compounds are usually hard crystalline solids; covalent compounds are often gases, liquids or soft solids
B1: electrovalent compounds have high melting and boiling points; covalent compounds usually have low ones
B1: electrovalent compounds conduct electricity when molten or in solution; covalent compounds generally do not
B1: electrovalent compounds usually dissolve in water; covalent compounds usually dissolve in organic solvents

questions.why: There are 7 horizontal periods and 18 vertical groups.

questions.q: An element with electronic configuration 2, 8, 7 is placed in
questions.why: Three shells give period 3; seven valence electrons put it in group 17 (it is chlorine).

long.q: State Mendeleev's periodic law and the modern periodic law.
scheme: B1: Mendeleev: the properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic masses
B1: modern: the properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers

long.q: Give two merits and one defect of Mendeleev's periodic table.
scheme: B1: he left gaps for elements not yet discovered and correctly predicted their properties (e.g. eka-aluminium, later gallium)
B1: he corrected the atomic masses of some elements, such as beryllium
B1: defect: the position of hydrogen was not fixed, or isotopes had no separate place, or some heavier elements came before lighter ones (e.g. argon and potassium)

long.q: State Newlands' law of octaves and give two of its limitations.
scheme: B1: when elements are arranged in increasing order of atomic mass, every eighth element has properties similar to the first, like the eighth note of a musical scale
B1: it held good only up to calcium
B1: newly discovered elements, such as the noble gases, could not be fitted into the arrangement

long.q: An element X has atomic number 12. State (a) its electronic configuration, (b) its period and group, (c) whether it is a metal or a non-metal, (d) the formula of its chloride.
scheme: B1: period 3, group 2
B1: a metal, because it loses two electrons easily
B1: XCl₂

long.q: Describe the main features of the modern periodic table with reference to groups 1, 17 and 18 and the positions of metals and non-metals.
scheme: B1: group 1 contains the alkali metals, with one valence electron; they are very reactive metals
B1: group 17 contains the halogens, with seven valence electrons; they are reactive non-metals
B1: group 18 contains the noble gases, with full outer shells; they are very unreactive
B1: metals lie on the left and in the centre, non-metals on the right, and metalloids along the zig-zag line between them

questions.q: In the laboratory, hydrogen is usually prepared from

nitric acid is a weak acid

questions.why: Hydrogen removes oxygen from copper(II) oxide, so it reduces it.

o: has one valence electron and can form a positive ion

questions.why: Like Na or K, it has one electron in its outer shell and can lose it to form H⁺.

long.q: Give one way in which hydrogen resembles the alkali metals and one way in which it resembles the halogens.
scheme: B1: like the alkali metals it has one valence electron, forms a positive ion (H⁺) and acts as a reducing agent
B1: like the halogens it needs one electron to complete its shell, can form a negative ion (H⁻, as in hydrides) and exists as diatomic molecules

long.q: Write balanced equations for the reaction that gives hydrogen from: (a) sodium and cold water, (b) zinc and hot concentrated sodium hydroxide solution, (c) magnesium and steam.
scheme: B1: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂
B1: Zn + 2NaOH → Na₂ZnO₂ + H₂
B1: Mg + H₂O → MgO + H₂

long.q: Describe the Bosch process for the large-scale manufacture of hydrogen, giving equations.
scheme: B1: steam is passed over white-hot coke at about 1000 °C to form water gas: C + H₂O → CO + H₂
B1: water gas mixed with excess steam is passed over iron(III) oxide catalyst (with chromium(III) oxide as promoter) at about 450 °C: CO + H₂O → CO₂ + H₂
B1: carbon dioxide is removed by dissolving it in water under pressure (about 30 atm)
B1: any carbon monoxide left is removed by passing the gas through ammoniacal copper(I) chloride solution
B1: fairly pure hydrogen remains

long.q: Describe in words the laboratory preparation of hydrogen, giving the equation, the method of collection with a reason, and a test for the gas.
scheme: B1: granulated zinc is placed in a flask and dilute hydrochloric acid is added through a thistle funnel: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂
B1: the gas passes through a delivery tube and is collected in a gas jar by the downward displacement of water
B1: it is collected over water because it is almost insoluble in water, and a mixture of hydrogen and air is explosive
B1: test: a lighted splint held at the mouth of a jar of the gas gives a pop sound

long.q: Define oxidation and reduction in terms of electrons. In the reaction Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu, identify the oxidising agent and the reducing agent.
scheme: B1: oxidation is the loss of electrons; reduction is the gain of electrons
B1: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻; zinc is oxidised, so zinc is the reducing agent
B1: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu; copper ions are reduced, so copper sulphate (Cu²⁺) is the oxidising agent

questions.q: Absolute zero is

questions.why: Charles's law: V ∝ T, so V–T is a straight line that passes through 0 K.

long.q: State Boyle's law and Charles's law.
scheme: B1: Boyle's law: at constant temperature, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure
B1: Charles's law: at constant pressure, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to its absolute (kelvin) temperature

long.q: A gas occupies 500 cm³ at a pressure of 760 mm of mercury. What will its volume be at 950 mm of mercury, the temperature remaining the same?
scheme: M1: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂
A1: V₂ = 400 cm³

scheme: A1: V₂ = 480 cm³

long.q: A gas has a volume of 380 cm³ at 27 °C and 800 mm of mercury. Calculate its volume at S.T.P.
scheme: B1: at S.T.P., T₂ = 273 K and P₂ = 760 mm of mercury
A1: V₂ = 364 cm³

long.q: Use the kinetic theory to explain: (a) why a gas exerts pressure; (b) why the pressure of a gas rises when it is heated in a closed container; (c) why the kelvin scale, not the Celsius scale, is used in Charles's law; (d) what would happen to the molecules at absolute zero.
scheme: B1: gas molecules move randomly at high speed and keep colliding with the walls, exerting a force on them
B1: on heating, the molecules move faster and hit the walls more often and harder, so the pressure rises
B1: volume is directly proportional to kelvin temperature; on the Celsius scale it is not (a gas at 0 °C still has volume)
B1: theoretically the molecules would have no kinetic energy and stop moving

questions.why: They dissolve in rainwater to form sulphuric and nitric acids.

long.q: State three harmful effects of acid rain.
scheme: B1: it corrodes buildings, monuments and metal structures, e.g. marble
B1: it makes lakes and soil acidic, killing fish and other aquatic life
B1: it washes nutrients out of the soil and damages leaves, harming crops and forests

long.q: Explain, with equations, how ozone forms in the stratosphere and how CFCs destroy it.
scheme: B1: ultraviolet radiation splits oxygen molecules into atoms: O₂ → O + O
B1: an oxygen atom combines with an oxygen molecule: O + O₂ → O₃
B1: ultraviolet radiation breaks CFCs to release chlorine atoms, e.g. CF₂Cl₂ → CF₂Cl + Cl
B1: Cl + O₃ → ClO + O₂, then ClO + O → Cl + O₂; the chlorine atom is set free again, so one atom can destroy many ozone molecules

long.q: Name the main source of each air pollutant: (a) carbon monoxide, (b) sulphur dioxide, (c) oxides of nitrogen, (d) methane.
scheme: B1: incomplete burning of fuels, especially in vehicle engines

B1: high-temperature combustion in vehicle engines and power stations (also lightning)
B1: paddy fields, cattle, and decaying waste in landfills

long.q: State three harmful effects on human beings of the depletion of the ozone layer.
scheme: B1: more ultraviolet radiation reaches the Earth, increasing skin cancer
B1: it causes eye damage such as cataracts
B1: it weakens the immune system (and damages crops and marine plankton)

questions.q: Across a period from left to right, the atomic size
questions.why: The nuclear charge increases while electrons enter the same shell, so they are pulled closer.

questions.q: The most electronegative element is
questions.why: Fluorine is small with a high nuclear pull on shared electrons; it heads the electronegativity scale.

questions.q: Going down group 1, the ionisation potential
questions.why: The atoms get larger and the outer electron is farther from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is removed more easily.

questions.q: Which element of period 3 is the most metallic?
questions.why: Metallic character decreases across a period; sodium, on the far left, loses its electron most easily.

questions.q: The energy released when a neutral gaseous atom gains an electron is called its
questions.why: Electron affinity measures the tendency of an isolated gaseous atom to accept an electron.

long.q: Define ionisation potential and state how it changes across a period.
scheme: B1: ionisation potential is the energy needed to remove an electron from the outermost shell of an isolated neutral gaseous atom
B1: it increases across a period, because the nuclear charge increases and the atomic size decreases

long.q: Give reasons: (a) the noble gases have practically zero electron affinity; (b) the atomic size of chlorine is smaller than that of sodium, though both are in period 3; (c) fluorine is more reactive than iodine.
scheme: B1: they have a stable, completely filled outer shell, so they have no tendency to accept an electron
B1: chlorine has a greater nuclear charge acting on the same number of shells, so its electrons are pulled closer
B1: fluorine is much smaller, so its nucleus attracts an incoming electron more strongly; its tendency to gain an electron is greater

long.q: Elements A, B and C have atomic numbers 9, 11 and 17. (a) Which two are in the same group? (b) Which is the most metallic? (c) Which has the largest atomic radius? (d) Write the formula of the compound formed between B and C and name the type of bond.
scheme: B1: A (2, 7) and C (2, 8, 7), both with seven valence electrons, are in group 17
B1: B (2, 8, 1) is the most metallic
B1: B has the largest atomic radius (it is in period 3 and on the left)
B1: BC, an electrovalent (ionic) compound
long.ans: A and C; B; B; BC, ionic

long.q: Describe how the following change down group 17 from fluorine to iodine: (a) atomic size, (b) electronegativity, (c) physical state at room temperature, (d) chemical reactivity.
scheme: B1: atomic size increases because a new shell is added at each step
B1: electronegativity decreases
B1: the state changes from gas (fluorine, chlorine) to liquid (bromine) to solid (iodine)
B1: reactivity decreases, as the larger atoms gain electrons less readily

long.q: Arrange as directed: (a) Cl, Na, P, Si in increasing order of ionisation potential; (b) Cs, Li, K, Na in increasing order of atomic size; (c) F, C, O, N in increasing order of electronegativity.
scheme: B1: Na < Si < P < Cl
B1: Li < Na < K < Cs
B1: C < N < O < F

questions.q: How many electrons are shared between the two atoms in a nitrogen molecule, N₂?
questions.why: N₂ has a triple bond: three shared pairs, i.e. six electrons.

questions.q: Which of these molecules is polar covalent?
questions.why: Chlorine is more electronegative than hydrogen, so the shared pair is pulled towards Cl; the others are non-polar.

questions.q: In the formation of the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺,
o: H⁺ donates an electron pair to nitrogen
nitrogen transfers an electron to hydrogen
nitrogen donates its lone pair to H⁺
two hydrogen atoms share a pair of electrons
questions.why: A coordinate bond forms when the lone pair on the nitrogen of NH₃ is shared with an H⁺ ion.

questions.q: How many lone pairs of electrons are there on the nitrogen atom in ammonia, NH₃?
questions.why: Nitrogen has five valence electrons: three are used in N–H bonds and two form one lone pair.

questions.q: Electrovalent compounds conduct electricity
o: when molten or dissolved in water
questions.why: The ions are fixed in the solid lattice but free to move when melted or in solution.

long.q: What is a coordinate bond? Give one example.
scheme: B1: a coordinate bond is a covalent bond in which the shared pair of electrons is donated by only one of the two atoms
B1: e.g. in the hydronium ion, H₃O⁺, the oxygen of water donates a lone pair to an H⁺ ion

long.q: Describe in words the bonding in carbon tetrachloride, CCl₄. Is the molecule polar? Why does it not conduct electricity?
scheme: B1: carbon (2, 4) shares one pair of electrons with each of four chlorine atoms, forming four single covalent bonds, so every atom has an octet
B1: the molecule is symmetrical (tetrahedral), so the bond polarities cancel and it is non-polar
B1: it is made of molecules with no free ions or electrons, so it does not conduct electricity

long.q: Describe the formation of calcium oxide from calcium (atomic number 20) and oxygen (atomic number 8) in terms of electron transfer, and show which change is oxidation and which is reduction.
scheme: B1: calcium (2, 8, 8, 2) loses two electrons: Ca → Ca²⁺ + 2e⁻; this is oxidation
B1: oxygen (2, 6) gains two electrons: O + 2e⁻ → O²⁻; this is reduction
B1: both ions now have a noble-gas configuration (argon and neon)
B1: the oppositely charged ions are held by strong electrostatic attraction, forming electrovalent CaO

long.q: Give reasons: (a) electrovalent compounds have high melting points; (b) covalent compounds such as sugar do not conduct electricity in solution; (c) water is a polar molecule.
scheme: B1: their oppositely charged ions are held in a lattice by strong electrostatic forces, which need a lot of energy to break
B1: they are made of molecules and do not form ions in water, so there are no charged particles to carry a current
B1: oxygen is more electronegative than hydrogen, so the shared pairs are pulled towards oxygen, giving it a partial negative charge; the bent shape stops the charges cancelling

long.q: Describe in words the formation of (a) the hydronium ion from water, (b) the ammonium ion from ammonia, stating the number of lone pairs left on the central atom in each ion.
scheme: B1: the oxygen atom in water has two lone pairs and donates one of them to an H⁺ ion, forming H₃O⁺
B1: one lone pair is left on oxygen in H₃O⁺
B1: the nitrogen atom in ammonia donates its single lone pair to an H⁺ ion, forming NH₄⁺
B1: no lone pair is left on nitrogen in NH₄⁺; once formed, all four N–H bonds are identical

long.q: Define an acid and an alkali in terms of the ions they produce in water.
scheme: B1: an acid is a compound which, when dissolved in water, gives hydronium ions (H₃O⁺) as the only positive ions
B1: an alkali is a base that dissolves in water and gives hydroxide ions (OH⁻) as the only negative ions

long.q: Distinguish between a strong acid and a concentrated acid, with an example of each.
scheme: B1: a strong acid ionises almost completely in water, e.g. hydrochloric acid
B1: a concentrated acid has a large amount of acid in a small amount of water, e.g. 98 % sulphuric acid
B1: the two ideas are different: concentrated (glacial) acetic acid is still a weak acid

long.q: Name the method and write a balanced equation to prepare: (a) zinc sulphate from zinc, (b) sodium chloride from sodium hydroxide, (c) barium sulphate, (d) copper sulphate from copper(II) oxide.
scheme: B1: action of a dilute acid on a metal: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂
B1: neutralisation by titration: NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O
B1: precipitation: BaCl₂ + Na₂SO₄ → BaSO₄ + 2NaCl
B1: action of an acid on an insoluble base: CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O

long.q: Solutions P, Q and R have pH values 1, 7 and 13. Which solution (a) turns methyl orange red (pink), (b) is neutral, (c) gives ammonia gas when warmed with ammonium chloride?
scheme: B1: P
B1: Q
B1: R

long.q: Give reasons: (a) a solution of hydrogen chloride in water conducts electricity but dry hydrogen chloride gas does not; (b) all alkalis are bases but not all bases are alkalis; (c) a solution of sodium carbonate is alkaline; (d) lead sulphate is not made by adding lead to dilute sulphuric acid.
scheme: B1: in water HCl ionises to give H₃O⁺ and Cl⁻ ions; dry HCl is a covalent gas with no ions
B1: an alkali is a base that dissolves in water; many bases, such as copper(II) oxide, are insoluble
B1: it is the salt of a strong base and a weak acid, so it reacts with water (hydrolysis) to give OH⁻ ions
B1: insoluble lead sulphate forms a coating on the lead, which stops the reaction

questions.q: A salt solution gives a reddish-brown precipitate with sodium hydroxide solution. The cation present is
questions.why: Iron(III) hydroxide, Fe(OH)₃, is reddish brown; iron(II) hydroxide is dirty green.

questions.q: Which cation gives a pale blue precipitate with ammonium hydroxide that dissolves in excess to form a deep (inky) blue solution?
questions.why: Cu(OH)₂ dissolves in excess ammonia to form a deep blue tetraamminecopper(II) complex.

questions.q: A cation gives a white precipitate with NaOH that dissolves in excess NaOH, and a white precipitate with NH₄OH that does NOT dissolve in excess. It is
questions.why: Both Zn(OH)₂ and Pb(OH)₂ dissolve in excess NaOH, but only Zn(OH)₂ dissolves in excess NH₄OH.

questions.q: The colour of a solution containing Fe²⁺ ions (e.g. iron(II) sulphate) is
questions.why: Fe²⁺ solutions are pale green; Fe³⁺ solutions are yellowish brown.

questions.q: Which of these is an amphoteric oxide?
questions.why: ZnO reacts with both acids and alkalis to form a salt and water; the others are basic.

long.q: What is an amphoteric oxide? Write an equation for the reaction of one with sodium hydroxide.
scheme: B1: an oxide that reacts with both acids and bases to form a salt and water
B1: ZnO + 2NaOH → Na₂ZnO₂ + H₂O

long.q: State what you observe when sodium hydroxide solution is added a little at a time and then in excess to (a) copper(II) sulphate solution, (b) iron(III) chloride solution. Write an equation for (a).
scheme: B1: (a) a pale blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide forms
B1: it does not dissolve in excess sodium hydroxide
B1: CuSO₄ + 2NaOH → Cu(OH)₂ + Na₂SO₄
B1: (b) a reddish-brown precipitate of iron(III) hydroxide forms, which does not dissolve in excess

long.q: How would you distinguish between the following pairs of solutions? (a) calcium nitrate and zinc nitrate, using ammonium hydroxide; (b) iron(II) sulphate and iron(III) sulphate, using sodium hydroxide; (c) lead nitrate and zinc nitrate, using ammonium hydroxide.
scheme: B1: zinc nitrate gives a white gelatinous precipitate that dissolves in excess; calcium nitrate gives no precipitate
B1: iron(II) sulphate gives a dirty green precipitate; iron(III) sulphate gives a reddish-brown precipitate
B1: both give white precipitates, but the zinc hydroxide dissolves in excess ammonium hydroxide while the lead hydroxide does not

long.q: Write balanced equations for the reactions of sodium hydroxide solution with: (a) zinc, (b) aluminium, (c) lead(II) oxide, (d) aluminium oxide.
scheme: B1: Zn + 2NaOH → Na₂ZnO₂ + H₂
B1: 2Al + 2NaOH + 2H₂O → 2NaAlO₂ + 3H₂
B1: PbO + 2NaOH → Na₂PbO₂ + H₂O
B1: Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH → 2NaAlO₂ + H₂O

long.q: Name the cation present in each case: (a) a dirty green precipitate with NaOH that slowly turns brown on standing in air; (b) a white precipitate with NaOH, insoluble in excess, but no precipitate with NH₄OH; (c) a blue solution that gives a pale blue precipitate with NaOH.
scheme: B1: Fe²⁺ (the iron(II) hydroxide is oxidised by air)
B1: Ca²⁺
B1: Cu²⁺

questions.q: The volume occupied by 2 moles of a gas at S.T.P. is
questions.why: One mole of any gas occupies 22.4 dm³ at S.T.P., so 2 moles occupy 44.8 dm³.

questions.q: The vapour density of a gas is 32. Its relative molecular mass is
questions.why: Relative molecular mass = 2 × vapour density = 64.

questions.q: Taking Avogadro's number as 6 × 10²³, the number of molecules in 18 g of water is
questions.why: 18 g of water (H₂O = 18) is one mole, which contains 6 × 10²³ molecules.

questions.q: The empirical formula of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, is
questions.why: Dividing by the common factor 6 gives the simplest whole-number ratio CH₂O.

questions.q: For 2CO + O₂ → 2CO₂, the volume of oxygen needed to burn 100 cm³ of carbon monoxide (same temperature and pressure) is
questions.why: By Gay-Lussac's law the volumes react in the ratio 2 : 1, so 100 cm³ of CO needs 50 cm³ of O₂.

long.q: State Avogadro's law and Gay-Lussac's law of combining volumes.
scheme: B1: Avogadro's law: equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain the same number of molecules

B1: Gay-Lussac's law: when gases react, they do so in volumes that bear a simple whole-number ratio to one another and to the volumes of gaseous products, all measured at the same temperature and pressure

long.q: A compound contains 40 % carbon, 6.67 % hydrogen and 53.33 % oxygen. Its vapour density is 30. Find its empirical formula and molecular formula. (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
scheme: M1: dividing by the smallest gives C : H : O = 1 : 2 : 1
A1: empirical formula = CH₂O (empirical formula mass 30)
M1: relative molecular mass = 2 × 30 = 60, so n = 60 ÷ 30 = 2
A1: molecular formula = C₂H₄O₂

long.q: Calcium carbonate decomposes on heating: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide formed from 25 g of calcium carbonate and its volume at S.T.P. (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)
scheme: B1: CaCO₃ = 100 and CO₂ = 44, so 100 g of CaCO₃ gives 44 g of CO₂
M1: mass of CO₂ = 25 × 44 ÷ 100
B1: 11 g is 0.25 mol, so volume = 0.25 × 22.4 = 5.6 dm³

long.q: Calculate the percentage of nitrogen in urea, CO(NH₂)₂. (C = 12, O = 16, N = 14, H = 1)
scheme: C1: relative molecular mass = 12 + 16 + 2 × (14 + 2) = 60

long.q: Propane burns according to the equation C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. 2 litres of propane are burnt in 15 litres of oxygen. Find the volume and composition of the gases left at the end, all volumes measured at room temperature and pressure (water is a liquid).
scheme: M1: by Gay-Lussac's law, propane, oxygen and carbon dioxide are in the ratio 1 : 5 : 3 by volume
A1: oxygen used = 2 × 5 = 10 litres, so 15 − 10 = 5 litres of oxygen is left
A1: carbon dioxide formed = 2 × 3 = 6 litres
B1: total volume of gas left = 5 + 6 = 11 litres (the water condenses to a liquid)
long.ans: 11 litres: 5 L oxygen + 6 L carbon dioxide

questions.q: During electrolysis, the cations move towards the
questions.why: Positive ions are attracted to the negative electrode, the cathode.

questions.q: During the electrolysis of molten lead bromide, the product at the anode is
questions.why: Br⁻ ions lose electrons at the anode: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻.

questions.q: Which of these is a non-electrolyte?
questions.why: Sugar is covalent and gives no ions in water.

questions.q: When an article is electroplated with silver, the article is made the
questions.why: Silver ions gain electrons and deposit as silver on the cathode.

questions.q: During the electrolysis of copper sulphate solution with copper electrodes, the anode
questions.why: The copper anode is active: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻, so it slowly dissolves.

long.q: Distinguish between electrolytic dissociation and ionisation, with one example of each.
scheme: B1: dissociation is the separation of ions already present in an ionic compound when it is melted or dissolved, e.g. NaCl → Na⁺ + Cl⁻
B1: ionisation is the formation of ions from a polar covalent compound when it dissolves in water, e.g. HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻

long.q: Water acidified with dilute sulphuric acid is electrolysed using platinum electrodes. Name the ions present, write the reactions at each electrode and give the ratio of the volumes of the gases formed.
scheme: B1: ions present: H⁺ (as H₃O⁺), OH⁻ and SO₄²⁻
B1: at the cathode: 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂
B1: at the anode OH⁻ is discharged in preference to SO₄²⁻: 4OH⁻ → 2H₂O + O₂ + 4e⁻
B1: hydrogen and oxygen are formed in the volume ratio 2 : 1

long.q: For the electrorefining of copper, name the anode, the cathode and the electrolyte, and write the reaction at each electrode. What happens to the impurities?
scheme: B1: anode: a block of impure copper; cathode: a thin sheet of pure copper; electrolyte: copper sulphate solution with a little dilute sulphuric acid
B1: anode: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻; cathode: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu
B1: the insoluble impurities collect below the anode as anode mud

long.q: A spoon is to be electroplated with nickel. Name the cathode, the anode and a suitable electrolyte, and explain why a small current is passed for a long time.
scheme: B1: cathode: the clean spoon
B1: anode: a block of pure nickel
B1: electrolyte: a solution of a nickel salt, such as nickel sulphate (or nickel ammonium sulphate)
B1: a small current deposits the metal slowly, giving an even, firmly sticking coat

long.q: Give reasons: (a) solid lead bromide does not conduct electricity but molten lead bromide does; (b) direct current, not alternating current, is used for electrolysis; (c) graphite electrodes are used in the electrolysis of molten lead bromide.
scheme: B1: in the solid the ions are held fixed in the lattice; on melting they become free to move
B1: alternating current keeps reversing, so the products would form at both electrodes alternately and mix
B1: graphite is inert and is not attacked by the bromine formed at the anode

questions.q: The chief ore of aluminium is
questions.why: Bauxite is hydrated aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃·2H₂O.

questions.q: Heating a sulphide ore strongly in excess air below its melting point, e.g. 2ZnS + 3O₂ → 2ZnO + 2SO₂, is called
questions.why: Roasting uses excess air; calcination is heating in little or no air, as for carbonates.

questions.q: Cryolite is added to alumina during its electrolysis to
o: raise the melting point of alumina
lower the fusion temperature and increase the conductivity
questions.why: Alumina dissolved in molten cryolite melts at about 950 °C instead of over 2000 °C and conducts better.

questions.q: Brass is an alloy of
questions.why: Copper and tin form bronze; lead and tin form solder.

questions.q: Froth flotation is used to concentrate
o: sulphide ores such as zinc blende
questions.why: Sulphide particles are wetted by oil and carried up in the froth, while the earthy gangue sinks.

long.q: Distinguish between a mineral and an ore.
scheme: B1: a mineral is a naturally occurring compound of a metal found in the earth's crust
B1: an ore is a mineral from which the metal can be extracted profitably and conveniently; all ores are minerals, but not all minerals are ores

long.q: Write balanced equations for the three main steps of Baeyer's process for purifying bauxite.
scheme: B1: bauxite is heated under pressure with concentrated sodium hydroxide: Al₂O₃·2H₂O + 2NaOH → 2NaAlO₂ + 3H₂O
B1: the sodium aluminate solution is diluted and seeded with a little aluminium hydroxide: NaAlO₂ + 2H₂O → NaOH + Al(OH)₃
B1: the aluminium hydroxide is heated to about 1000 °C: 2Al(OH)₃ → Al₂O₃ + 3H₂O

long.q: Describe the electrolytic extraction of aluminium (Hall–Héroult process): the electrolyte and temperature, the electrodes, the reactions at each electrode, and why the anodes must be replaced from time to time.
scheme: B1: electrolyte: pure alumina dissolved in molten cryolite with a little fluorspar, at about 950 °C
B1: cathode: the carbon lining of the steel tank; anode: thick graphite rods dipping into the melt
B1: at the cathode: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al, and molten aluminium collects at the bottom
B1: at the anode: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻
B1: the oxygen reacts with the hot graphite to form carbon dioxide, so the anodes burn away and must be replaced

long.q: Give the main constituents and one use of: (a) duralumin, (b) solder, (c) stainless steel.
scheme: B1: duralumin: aluminium with copper, magnesium and manganese; used for aircraft bodies
B1: solder: lead and tin; used for joining electrical wires (it has a low melting point)
B1: stainless steel: iron with chromium and nickel (and a little carbon); used for utensils and surgical instruments

long.q: (a) Why is aluminium extracted by electrolysis and not by reduction with carbon? (b) Why is aluminium used for overhead electric cables? (c) Write the equation for the calcination of calamine. (d) Write the equation for the reduction of zinc oxide with coke.
scheme: B1: aluminium is high in the reactivity series and has a strong affinity for oxygen, so carbon cannot reduce aluminium oxide
B1: it is a good conductor, light in weight and resists corrosion because of its protective oxide layer
B1: ZnCO₃ → ZnO + CO₂
B1: ZnO + C → Zn + CO

questions.q: In the laboratory preparation of hydrogen chloride, the gas is dried by passing it through
questions.why: HCl is acidic, so it reacts with basic drying agents such as quicklime; concentrated H₂SO₄ does not react with it.

questions.q: Hydrogen chloride gas is collected by
questions.why: It is heavier than air and very soluble in water, so it is collected with the jar upright, pushing the air upwards.

questions.q: Aqua regia is a mixture of
o: 1 part concentrated HCl and 3 parts concentrated HNO₃
3 parts concentrated HCl and 1 part concentrated HNO₃
equal parts of HCl and H₂SO₄
questions.why: Three volumes of concentrated hydrochloric acid with one of concentrated nitric acid; it dissolves gold and platinum.

questions.q: The fountain experiment with hydrogen chloride shows that the gas
questions.why: A little water dissolves so much gas that the pressure in the flask drops and water rushes in as a fountain.

questions.q: When silver nitrate solution is added to dilute hydrochloric acid,
o: a curdy white precipitate insoluble in nitric acid forms
questions.why: AgNO₃ + HCl → AgCl + HNO₃; silver chloride is a curdy white precipitate.

long.q: Write the equation for the laboratory preparation of hydrogen chloride and state why the temperature is kept below about 200 °C.
scheme: B1: NaCl + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HCl
B1: at higher temperature sodium sulphate forms as a hard crust that sticks to the flask and is hard to remove (and more fuel is used)

long.q: Give reasons: (a) hydrogen chloride is not collected over water; (b) hydrogen chloride fumes in moist air; (c) an inverted funnel is used when dissolving hydrogen chloride gas in water.
scheme: B1: it is extremely soluble in water
B1: it dissolves in the moisture of the air to form tiny droplets of hydrochloric acid
B1: the funnel prevents back suction of water into the apparatus and gives a large surface for the gas to dissolve

long.q: Write balanced equations for the reaction of dilute hydrochloric acid with: (a) zinc, (b) sodium sulphite, (c) iron(II) sulphide, (d) lead nitrate solution.
scheme: B1: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂
B1: Na₂SO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + SO₂
B1: FeS + 2HCl → FeCl₂ + H₂S
B1: Pb(NO₃)₂ + 2HCl → PbCl₂ + 2HNO₃

long.q: Describe in words the fountain experiment with hydrogen chloride gas and state what it shows.
scheme: B1: a dry round-bottomed flask is filled with dry hydrogen chloride and closed with a cork carrying a long jet tube
B1: the flask is held upside down with the jet dipping into a trough of water coloured with blue litmus
B1: when a little water enters, the gas dissolves, the pressure inside falls, and water rushes up through the jet as a fountain
B1: the blue litmus turns red, showing that hydrogen chloride is highly soluble and forms an acidic solution

long.q: Give three tests to identify hydrogen chloride gas.
scheme: B1: a glass rod dipped in ammonia solution held near the gas gives dense white fumes of ammonium chloride: NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl
B1: it turns moist blue litmus paper red
B1: passed into silver nitrate solution, it gives a curdy white precipitate of silver chloride

questions.q: Ammonia gas is dried using
questions.why: Ammonia is basic, so it reacts with acidic drying agents and forms a compound with calcium chloride.

questions.q: The catalyst used in the Haber process is
questions.why: Iron, with molybdenum as a promoter, speeds up N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃.

questions.q: Ammonia is collected by
questions.why: It is lighter than air and very soluble in water, so it is collected in an inverted jar.

questions.q: When ammonia is passed over heated copper(II) oxide, the black solid turns
questions.why: Ammonia reduces CuO to copper, which is reddish brown.

questions.q: Liquid ammonia is used in refrigeration because it
o: has a high latent heat of vaporisation
questions.why: It absorbs a lot of heat from the surroundings when it evaporates.

long.q: Write the equation for the laboratory preparation of ammonia from ammonium chloride, and state why the flask is fitted in a sloping position.
scheme: B1: 2NH₄Cl + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCl₂ + 2H₂O + 2NH₃
B1: so that the water formed does not run back onto the hot part of the flask and crack it

long.q: Give the equation and the conditions for the Haber process, and explain why a temperature of about 450–500 °C is used even though a lower temperature gives a better yield.
scheme: B1: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ + heat, the gases mixed in the ratio 1 : 3 by volume
B1: pressure of about 200–900 atm and a temperature of 450–500 °C
B1: catalyst: finely divided iron with molybdenum as a promoter
B1: at a lower temperature the reaction would be too slow, so a compromise temperature is used; the ammonia is removed by cooling it to a liquid

long.q: Write balanced equations for: (a) the burning of ammonia in oxygen, (b) the catalytic oxidation of ammonia, naming the catalyst, (c) the reaction of excess ammonia with chlorine.
scheme: B1: 4NH₃ + 3O₂ → 2N₂ + 6H₂O
B1: 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O, with platinum at about 800 °C
B1: 8NH₃ + 3Cl₂ → 6NH₄Cl + N₂

long.q: Dry ammonia is passed over heated copper(II) oxide. State what you observe, write the equation, and explain how the water formed and the gas collected can be identified.
scheme: B1: the black copper(II) oxide turns reddish brown
B1: 3CuO + 2NH₃ → 3Cu + 3H₂O + N₂
B1: the colourless liquid that condenses turns white anhydrous copper sulphate blue, showing it is water
B1: the gas collected is nitrogen, which neither burns nor supports burning; ammonia acts as a reducing agent

long.q: Give reasons: (a) ammonia is not dried with concentrated sulphuric acid; (b) aqueous ammonia turns red litmus blue; (c) liquid ammonia and liquor ammonia are different.
scheme: B1: ammonia is basic and reacts with the acid: 2NH₃ + H₂SO₄ → (NH₄)₂SO₄
B1: it forms ammonium hydroxide in water, which gives OH⁻ ions
B1: liquid ammonia is pure ammonia liquefied by cooling and pressure; liquor ammonia is a concentrated solution of ammonia in water

questions.q: Concentrated nitric acid often looks yellow because of dissolved
questions.why: The acid slowly decomposes in light, and the brown NO₂ formed dissolves in it.

questions.q: The catalyst in the Ostwald process is
questions.why: Ammonia is oxidised to nitric oxide over hot platinum gauze.

questions.q: Copper reacts with dilute nitric acid to give
questions.why: 3Cu + 8HNO₃ → 3Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO + 4H₂O; concentrated acid gives NO₂ instead.

questions.q: An all-glass apparatus is used in the laboratory preparation of nitric acid because
o: nitric acid vapour attacks rubber and cork
questions.why: Hot nitric acid vapour is highly corrosive and would destroy rubber or cork stoppers.

questions.q: Metals generally do not give hydrogen with nitric acid because nitric acid
o: is a strong oxidising agent that oxidises the hydrogen to water
questions.why: Any hydrogen formed is oxidised at once, and oxides of nitrogen are given off instead.

long.q: Write the equation for the laboratory preparation of nitric acid from potassium nitrate, and state why the temperature is kept below about 200 °C.
scheme: B1: KNO₃ + H₂SO₄ → KHSO₄ + HNO₃
B1: at higher temperatures nitric acid decomposes into nitrogen dioxide, and the potassium sulphate formed would cake hard in the retort

long.q: Write the three equations for the manufacture of nitric acid by the Ostwald process, with the conditions for the first step.
scheme: B1: 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O, over platinum gauze at about 800 °C, using ammonia and air in the ratio of about 1 : 10 by volume
B1: on cooling, 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂
B1: in the absorption tower, 4NO₂ + 2H₂O + O₂ → 4HNO₃
B1: the first reaction is exothermic, so once started the catalyst stays hot without further heating

long.q: Write balanced equations for the reactions of: (a) concentrated nitric acid with copper, (b) concentrated nitric acid with carbon, (c) concentrated nitric acid with sulphur, (d) dilute nitric acid with copper.
scheme: B1: Cu + 4HNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO₂ + 2H₂O
B1: C + 4HNO₃ → CO₂ + 4NO₂ + 2H₂O
B1: S + 6HNO₃ → H₂SO₄ + 6NO₂ + 2H₂O
B1: 3Cu + 8HNO₃ → 3Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO + 4H₂O

long.q: Explain why concentrated nitric acid turns yellow on standing, write the equation, and state how the colour can be removed.
scheme: B1: the acid slowly decomposes in light or on warming
B1: 4HNO₃ → 4NO₂ + 2H₂O + O₂; the reddish-brown NO₂ dissolves in the acid and makes it yellow
B1: the colour is removed by bubbling dry air or carbon dioxide through the warm acid (or by adding water)

long.q: State what you observe when: (a) concentrated nitric acid is added to copper turnings; (b) dilute nitric acid is added to copper turnings in a test tube; (c) sulphur is heated with concentrated nitric acid.
scheme: B1: reddish-brown fumes of nitrogen dioxide are given off and the solution turns blue
B1: a colourless gas (nitric oxide) is given off, which turns reddish brown at the mouth of the tube as it reacts with air; the solution turns blue
B1: reddish-brown fumes are given off and the sulphur is oxidised to sulphuric acid (the solution then gives a white precipitate with barium chloride)

questions.q: The catalyst used in the Contact process is
questions.why: V₂O₅ catalyses 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ at about 450 °C.

questions.q: Sulphur trioxide is dissolved in concentrated sulphuric acid rather than in water because
o: sulphur trioxide is insoluble in water
with water it forms a dense mist of acid droplets that is hard to condense
questions.why: The reaction with water is so violent that a fog of acid forms; dissolving it in H₂SO₄ to make oleum avoids this.

questions.q: Concentrated sulphuric acid turns sugar black. This shows its
questions.why: It removes the elements of water from sugar, leaving carbon: C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ → 12C + 11H₂O.

questions.q: The formula of oleum is
questions.why: Oleum (pyrosulphuric acid) forms when SO₃ dissolves in concentrated H₂SO₄.

questions.q: Concentrated sulphuric acid is used to prepare hydrogen chloride and nitric acid from their salts because it is
o: non-volatile (it has a high boiling point)
questions.why: A less volatile acid displaces a more volatile acid from its salt.

long.q: Why must concentrated sulphuric acid be added slowly to water, and never water to the acid?
scheme: B1: dissolving the acid in water gives out a great deal of heat
B1: if water is added to the acid, it boils at once and the acid spurts out; adding acid slowly to water with stirring spreads the heat safely

long.q: Write the equations for the main steps of the Contact process and give the conditions for the catalytic step.
scheme: B1: S + O₂ → SO₂ (or by roasting iron pyrites)
B1: 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ + heat, with vanadium pentoxide catalyst at about 450 °C and 1–2 atm
B1: SO₃ + H₂SO₄ → H₂S₂O₇
B1: H₂S₂O₇ + H₂O → 2H₂SO₄

long.q: Write balanced equations to show concentrated sulphuric acid acting as an oxidising agent with: (a) copper, (b) carbon, (c) sulphur.
scheme: B1: Cu + 2H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + SO₂ + 2H₂O
B1: C + 2H₂SO₄ → CO₂ + 2SO₂ + 2H₂O
B1: S + 2H₂SO₄ → 3SO₂ + 2H₂O

long.q: Name the property of sulphuric acid shown in each case: (a) Zn + H₂SO₄ (dil) → ZnSO₄ + H₂; (b) C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ → 12C + 11H₂O; (c) NaCl + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HCl; (d) its use for drying chlorine gas.
scheme: B1: acidic property (dilute acid with an active metal)
B1: dehydrating property
B1: non-volatile nature (a less volatile acid displaces a more volatile one)
B1: hygroscopic nature (it absorbs moisture)

long.q: Show, with equations, that dilute sulphuric acid is a dibasic acid.
scheme: B1: each molecule has two replaceable hydrogen ions, so it can form two kinds of salt
B1: NaOH + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + H₂O (acid salt)
B1: 2NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O (normal salt)

questions.q: The general formula of the alkenes is
questions.why: Alkenes have one C=C double bond, e.g. ethene C₂H₄.

questions.q: The IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂OH is
questions.why: Two carbon atoms (eth-), single bonds (-an-) and an –OH group (-ol).

questions.q: An unsaturated hydrocarbon can be detected because it decolourises
questions.why: Bromine adds across the double or triple bond, so its orange-brown colour disappears.

questions.q: How many structural isomers does butane, C₄H₁₀, have?
questions.why: n-butane (straight chain) and 2-methylpropane (branched chain).

questions.q: The reaction of methane with chlorine in diffused sunlight is a
questions.why: A hydrogen atom is replaced by chlorine: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl.

long.q: What is a homologous series? Give two of its characteristics.
scheme: B1: a series of organic compounds with the same functional group and general formula, in which each member differs from the next by a CH₂ group
B1: members have similar chemical properties and show a gradation in physical properties; their molecular masses differ by 14

long.q: Give the IUPAC names of: (a) CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO, (b) CH₃COOH, (c) CH₃CH=CHCH₃.
scheme: B1: butanal
B1: ethanoic acid
B1: but-2-ene

long.q: Write the equation and conditions for the preparation of ethene from ethanol. Give equations for the addition of (a) bromine and (b) hydrogen to ethene, and state how bromine can distinguish ethene from ethane.
scheme: B1: C₂H₅OH → C₂H₄ + H₂O, by heating with excess concentrated sulphuric acid at about 170 °C
B1: C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂ (1,2-dibromoethane)
B1: C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆, with a nickel catalyst at about 300 °C
B1: ethene decolourises bromine water; ethane, being saturated, does not

long.q: Describe in words the structural formulae of the two isomers of C₄H₁₀ and name them. What kind of isomerism is this?
scheme: B1: n-butane (butane): four carbon atoms in a straight chain, CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃
B1: isobutane (2-methylpropane): a chain of three carbon atoms with a CH₃ branch on the middle carbon, CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₃
B1: they have the same molecular formula but different arrangements of the carbon chain: chain isomerism

long.q: Ethanoic acid is warmed with ethanol and a few drops of concentrated sulphuric acid. Write the equation, state the role of the sulphuric acid and what you would notice, and give a test to show that ethanoic acid is an acid.
scheme: B1: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O (ethyl ethanoate is formed)
B1: concentrated sulphuric acid acts as a catalyst and dehydrating agent
B1: a sweet, fruity smell of the ester is noticed
B1: with sodium hydrogencarbonate it gives brisk effervescence of carbon dioxide: CH₃COOH + NaHCO₃ → CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂
